Looking at this problem, I need to determine whether the "generating" property (jointly faithful condition) implies the existence of an epimorphism from a coproduct of generators onto any object.

## Answer: Yes, it is true.

**Construction.** Let \(X \in \mathcal{A}\) be any object. Consider the collection of all morphisms from objects in \(\mathcal{P}\) to \(X\):

$$I = \{(P, p) : P \in \mathcal{P},\; p: P \to X \text{ is a morphism in } \mathcal{A}\}.$$

For each \(i = (P, p) \in I\), set \(P_i = P\). Since \(\mathcal{A}\) contains all (small) colimits, the coproduct \(\bigoplus_{i \in I} P_i\) exists — the index set \(I\) is a set when \(\mathcal{P}\) is a set (the standard convention for a generating set), since each \(\mathrm{Hom}(P, X)\) is a set by local smallness and the disjoint union of set-many sets is a set.

Define the **canonical map**:

$$\varphi: \bigoplus_{i \in I} P_i \longrightarrow X$$

by setting the component corresponding to \(i = (P, p)\) to be \(p\) itself, i.e., \(\varphi \circ \iota_i = p\) for each \(i = (P,p)\), where \(\iota_i: P_i \hookrightarrow \bigoplus_{i\in I} P_i\) is the coproduct injection. This is well-defined by the universal property of the coproduct.

**Verification that \(\varphi\) is an epimorphism.** Let \(f, g: X \to Y\) be two morphisms such that \(f \circ \varphi = g \circ \varphi\). Then for each \(i = (P, p) \in I\):

$$f \circ \varphi \circ \iota_i = g \circ \varphi \circ \iota_i \implies f \circ p = g \circ p.$$

This holds for **every** morphism \(p: P \to X\) with \(P \in \mathcal{P}\). By the generating property of \(\mathcal{P}\) (as defined in the problem — jointly faithful), we conclude \(f = g\). Therefore \(\varphi\) is an epimorphism. \(\square\)

**Two remarks:**

1. **Size issues.** The index set \(I\) is the disjoint union \(\coprod_{P \in \mathcal{P}} \mathrm{Hom}(P, X)\). If \(\mathcal{P}\) is a set (the usual convention for a "generating set of objects"), then \(I\) is a set and the coproduct exists since \(\mathcal{A}\) has all small colimits. If \(\mathcal{P}\) is a proper class, one needs the additional assumption that the relevant coproduct exists, or that a set-sized subfamily of \(\mathcal{P}\) already generates.

2. **Projectivity is not needed here.** The projectivity of the objects in \(\mathcal{P}\) plays no role in this result — it is used for subsequent constructions (e.g., building projective resolutions, where one iterates this construction on kernels). The existence of the epimorphism from a coproduct of generators relies solely on the generating (jointly faithful) property and the existence of coproducts.
